Volatile solves visibility problem i.e if any thread has updated variable then other thread should get this updated value
before reading them.
Usually each core has its own local cache so when a thread updates variable its only updated in local cache.. other core running another thread using same variable is not aware that variable is changed so volatile pushes changes to shared memory ( cache ) and then its updated in other core also so now when other thread tries to read same variable it gets updated value

volatile boolean flag = true;
Now volatile doesn't synchronizes threads.. so many thread can write simulatinously, and for eg. incrementing a variable is not a single task, it has 2 tasks like first reading variable and then incrementing it and then writing it back, so as we have many cores
one thread might update variable while other thread will use old value and then do its thing.. so there is no synchronization here..
So how we solve this ?
1) Use synchronized (but this is slow..):
2) AtomicInteger :

we have to either use locks ( which is slow ) or synchronized (slow.. ) or we can also create object for every sub task while processing req. which may consume resources fast..

So threadlocal is used here ( no synchronization needed.. )
So after response is served we must clear threadlocal so that thread can server new req. :

Parallelism means executing independent task simultaneously at a time. while concurrency means executing tasks in time sharing manner. eg There is parallelism while processing multiple user's request. ( as they are independent )
while there is concurrency while booking a ticket as operation is dependent on other's actions..
As parallelism is for independent tasks we don;t need to do anything special for this.

Condition Class ( its a wait notify alternative for explicit locks.. as wait notify is only for implicit or synchronized block.. )
Now as we know wait and notify is used to signal threads that are waiting for lock.. but wait and notify is only for intrinsic locks i.e
they can be only used with synchronized block.
So in Java 5, java added extrinsic locks i.e explicit Locks so we need something like wait & notify.. so Java added Condition class, which does similar but wait and notify is just one condition what if we want multiple conditions and want to tell only those threads which want to be notified for specific conditions only ?? so with this new Condition class we can create many conditions we want.. ( of course with explicit locks only.. )

Tread t1 & t2 will use readlock first and t3 & t4 will be in wait state..
after t1,t2 read completes then t3 gets write lock.. and after it completes then t4

Runnable vs Callable
 A Runnable, however, does not return a result and cannot throw a checked exception.
Runnable has been around since Java 1.0, but Callable was only introduced in Java 1.5 ...
to handle use-cases that Runnable does not support. In theory, the Java team could have
changed the signature of the Runnable.run() method, but this would have broken binary
compatiblity with pre-1.5 code, requiring recoding when migrating old Java code to newer JVMs.
 That is a BIG NO-NO.
java.util.concurrent.Future.get() will throw ExecutionException
if provided callable threw exception in the past (the exception is stored in the Future).
Exception thrown when attempting to retrieve the result of a task that aborted by throwing an exception.
 This exception can be inspected using the Throwable.getCause() method.
Does a Future timeout kill the Thread execution ? i.e whether calling get on future with timeout
(so that we wait for only some time..)
it does not. Why would it? Unless you tell it to.
There is a very valid concern here in case of a Callable for example. If you waited for the result for say 20 seconds and you did not get it, then you are not interested in the result anymore. At that time you should cancel the task at all.
Something like this:
Future<?> future = service.submit(new MyCallable());
   try {
       future.get(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
   } catch (Exception e){
       e.printStackTrace();
       future.cancel(true); //this method will stop the running underlying task
   }

Thread Pools
As we can't just go on create thread for every task as we have limited resources so we can create limited threads that execute all those tasks.
Executors is a factory to create thread pool implementations
ExecutorService has many methods to control and terminate services, this accepts both Runnable ( via execute )
and Callable( via submit )
eg.
ExecutorService executorService = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
Future<String> future = executorService.submit(() -> "Hello World");
// some operations
String result = future.get(); //this is blocking call
Here are the type of thread pools you can create with the Executors class :
  *  Single Thread Executor : A thread pool with only one thread. So all the submitted tasks will be executed sequentially. Method : Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()
  *  Cached Thread Pool : A thread pool that creates as many threads it needs to execute the task in parallel. The old available threads will be reused for the new tasks. If a thread is not used during 60 seconds, it will be terminated and removed from the pool. Method : Executors.newCachedThreadPool() ( unbounded thread pool , as this has no bounds on max threads, so Integer.MAX_VALUE no of threads can be created )
  *  Fixed Thread Pool : A thread pool with a fixed number of threads. If a thread is not available for the task, the task is put in queue waiting for an other task to ends. Method : Executors.newFixedThreadPool()
  *  Scheduled Thread Pool : A thread pool made to schedule future task. Method : Executors.newScheduledThreadPool() ( unbounded thread pool , as this has no bounds on max threads, so Integer.MAX_VALUE no of threads can be created )
  *  Single Thread Scheduled Pool : A thread pool with only one thread to schedule future task.
Method : Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()
  *  WorkStealingPool : This is a Fork Join Pool
SingleThreadExecutor (when we want tasks to be processed sequentially) :
ScheduledExecutorService :
ThreadPoolExecutor ( FixedThreadPool )
( suitable for general purpose and long running tasks )
ThreadPoolExecutor executor = (ThreadPoolExecutor) Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);
In this manner, the thread pool is pre configured for the most common cases. The number of threads can be controlled by setting the parameters:
  *  corePoolSize and maximumPoolSize – which represent the bounds of the number of threads
  *  keepAliveTime – which determines the time to keep extra threads alive
  *  
If a task is submitted and fewer than corePoolSize threads are in execution, then a new thread is created. The same thing happens if there are more than [corePoolSize] but less than [maximumPoolSize] threads running, and the task queue is full. If there are more than [corePoolSize] threads, which have been idle for longer than [keepAliveTime], they will be terminated.
CachedThreadPool :
( this is suitable for short lived tasks only, doesn't maintains minimum threads.. if thread is idle for 1 min its killed )
In FixedThreadPool only max threads can be created specified at the time of creation of pool, if threads are busy then tasks put in LinkedBlockingQueue for waiting.. but in case of CachedThreadPool task is executed as soon as its submited.. there is no waiting area
and maximum number of threads that can be created is only limited by system resources and ( Integer.MAX_VALUE )
so,
The cached pool starts with zero threads and can potentially grow to have Integer.MAX_VALUE threads. Practically, the only limitation for a cached thread pool is the available system resources. To better manage system resources, cached thread pools will remove threads that remain idle for one minute.
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
executor.submit(task);
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Advanced Thread Pool Options:
Internally every thread pool type uses ThreadPoolExecutor :
Here 0 mean not applicable
Why not ArrayBlockingQueue, why LinkedBlockingQueue??
Because ArrayBlockingQueue has fixed size and we want unlimited tasks can be queued so that we should not create more threads.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
What do you mean by thread pools reuse threads :
Thread pools dont reuse threads by calling start multiple times on same thread object.. start can be only called once..
So every thread pool maintains a queue for pending tasks and worker threads gets tasks from that queue and execute them.
& if there are no tasks then they wait for it. Usually Blocking Queue is used as task queue.
Pseudo code:
while (!pool.isShutdown()) {
    Runnable task = pool.waitForTaskOnQueue();
    task.run();
}
How to shutdown the thread pool :
call shutdown() to stop accepting new tasks.. if we try to add task after this then it will throw Exception
then wait for thread pool to terminate by calling awaitTermination(long timeout, TimeUnit unit)
after above timeout call shutdownNow() to interrupt running threads and try to terminate thread pool
( if we call shutdownNow() before awaitTermination(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) then awaitTermination doesn't play any role as 
we have already tried to kill threads and stop thread pool, no error or exception but its useless )
void shutdown();
List<Runnable> shutdownNow();
boolean awaitTermination(long timeout, TimeUnit unit);
final ExecutorService executor;
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread() {
    public void run() {
        executor.shutdown();
        if (!executor.awaitTermination(SHUTDOWN_TIME)) { //optional *
            Logger.log("Executor did not terminate in the specified time."); //optional *
            List<Runnable> droppedTasks = executor.shutdownNow(); //optional **
            Logger.log("Executor was abruptly shut down. " + droppedTasks.size() + " tasks will not be executed."); //optional **
        }
    }
});

Annotations:
  *  @Test - normal test annotation

  *  @MockBean - just a marker for bean to mock
  *  @InjectMocks - marker for Bean in which we / framework will inject mock
JUnit
Mockito
Why we need mockito ??
Well as in Unit testing we only test specific code logic & not the underlaying components logic as that is Integration testing so we are not testing others code we only test ours, so we need to mock out other components which our code uses so we can either create stubs which is dummy code in that we will create dummy implemention classes which is tedious so here we can use mockito to mock components with just simple line of code , no need to implement or create dummy classes..
Steps:
  *  import mockito static methods
  *  create mock of objects : SomeDataService ds = mock(SomeDataService.class)
  *  implements / mock required method eg. when(ds.getData()).thenReturn(new int[] {1,2,3});
  *  Now set manually to your business service
@Before
instead of duplicating code in every test we can move common code to @Before
So instead of creating objects manually & setting mocked dependency manually, we can do that automatically just by adding annotation
  *  @RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)
  *  @InjectMocks on object in which we want to inject mocked object
  *  @Mock : just marks object needs to be mocked & to be injected in some object
If we just say when(mockobj.size()) & dont specify return then default values are returned
we can also specify multiple return values so on first invocation first return value , one second.. second invocation value..
Argument Matchers :
we can specify argument matchers so that to handle generic methods
Types of Args Matchers available in Mockito class , all are static methods
Verify Method calls, how many times it called.. :
Argument Capture:
We can also capture arguments passed to mock methods
verify(mock)... only matches method execution 1 times so if we are calling it multiple times then we need to specify that
Spy :
Now mocking doesn't calls original object methods it mocks all, method we are interested in we use when(mockobj.method()).then..
all other methods where we dont specify when..then.. return default values specified by Mickito
When we want original object behaviour and only want to override some specific methods then use spy
  *  Use @Mock when you want to just test the functionality externally without actually calling that method.
  *  Use @Spy when you want to test the functionality externally + internally.
  *  Mock object replace mocked class entirely, returning recorded or default values. You can create mock out of "thin air". This is what is mostly used during unit testing. 
  *  When spying, you take an existing object and "replace" only some methods. This is useful when you have a huge class and only want to mock certain methods (partial mocking)
Mockito Limitations :
There is powermock library which provides these functions which mockito doesn't support like static methods , private methods..

Why blocking queue is different than notify(),wait()..
The notify(), wait() all depends on lock to operate on.. which is slow
but blocking queue does this all with the help of CAS intructions, which are atomic and non blocking
so every collection in java.util.concurrent is a lock free collection
which will be always faster than other non.. collections..
====================================================================
Blocking Queue ( solves producer - consumer problem )
Blocking Queue is thread safe, now as name suggest it blocks thread in get or put operation but it provides multiple methods or blocking or non blocking behavior.
For instance, if a thread tries to take an element and there are none left in the queue, the thread can be blocked until there is an element to take. Whether or not the calling thread is blocked depends on what methods you call on the BlockingQueue.
Now this Queue 4 different set of methods with different behavior :
Now (Un) bounded means initially unbounded but we can make them bounded by specifying size in constructor
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Delay Queue
It has a very useful characteristic – when the consumer wants to take an element from the queue, they can take it only when the delay for that particular element has expired.
Implementing Delayed for Elements in the DelayQueue:
( need to have constructor which takes delay in millisec. , getDelay() which returns how much time left, compareTo() to order elements according to delay remaining, head will have least delay element and tail will have highest delay element )
Each element we want to put into the DelayQueue needs to implement the Delayed interface.
We'll pass the String data and delayInMilliseconds as and arguments to its constructor:
public class DelayObject implements Delayed {
    private String data;
    private long startTime;
 
    public DelayObject(String data, long delayInMilliseconds) {
        this.data = data;
        this.startTime = System.currentTimeMillis() + delayInMilliseconds;
}
We are defining a startTime – this is a time when the element should be consumed from the queue. 
Next, we need to implement the getDelay() method – it should return the remaining delay associated with this object in the given time unit.
Therefore, we need to use the TimeUnit.convert() method to return the remaining delay in the proper TimeUnit:
@Override
public long getDelay(TimeUnit unit) {
    long diff = startTime - System.currentTimeMillis();
    return unit.convert(diff, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}
When the consumer tries to take an element from the queue, 
the DelayQueue will execute getDelay() to find out if that element is allowed to be returned from the queue. If the getDelay() method will return zero or a negative number, it means that it could be retrieved from the queue.
We also need to implement the compareTo() method, because the elements in the DelayQueue will be sorted according to the expiration time. The item that will expire first is kept at the head of the queue and the element with the highest expiration time is kept at the tail of the queue:
@Override
public int compareTo(Delayed o) {
    return Ints.saturatedCast(
      this.startTime - ((DelayObject) o).startTime);
}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PriorityBlockingQueue :
Its a sorted queue based on priority uses compareTo (elements implements this) or comparator ( in constructor so elements no need to implement comparable ) so sort elements according to priority.
Iterator does not guarantee to iterate the elements in priority order.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Synchronous Queue :
The SynchronousQueue is a queue that can only contain a single element internally. 
A thread inseting an element into the queue is blocked until another thread takes that element from the queue.
 Likewise, if a thread tries to take an element and no element is currently present, that thread is blocked until a thread insert an element into the queue.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

===========================================================================================================
ConcurrentMapConcurrentHashMap :
The ConcurrentHashMap is very similar to the java.util.HashTable class, except that ConcurrentHashMap offers better concurrency than HashTable does. 
ConcurrentHashMap does not lock the Map while you are reading from it. Additionally, ConcurrentHashMap does not lock the entire Map when writing to it. It only locks the part of the Map that is being written to, internally.
Another difference is that ConcurrentHashMap does not throw ConcurrentModificationException if the ConcurrentHashMap is changed while being iterated. The Iterator is not designed to be used by more than one thread and may(same word is in javadocs) not see the changes in map if its modified concurrently..
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ConcurrentSkipListMap : same as ConcurrentHashMap but its sorted ( like Treemap )
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CopyOnWriteArrayList : Its concurrent version of ArrayList, but its very expensive for write operations.. as for every write a new copy of existing list is made and element is added to it. similarly CopyOnWriteArraySet works.
Iterator of CopyOnWriteArrayList is fail-safe and doesn't throw ConcurrentModificationException even if underlying CopyOnWriteArrayList is modified once Iteration begins because Iterator is operating on separate copy of ArrayList. Consequently all the updates made on CopyOnWriteArrayList is not available to Iterator.
You should only use this read when you are doing upwards of 90+% reads.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So how the fail fast behavior works in Non-Thread safe Collections ??
Those collections have internal variable that counts modification made, now iterator before getting each element checks modcount with its own copy that it created before starting iteration so if its mismatch then modification has happened while iterating, then it just throws exception..
Now as Thread safe collection iterators work on copy of collection i.e snapshot of collection.. they will not reflect any changes made to original /actual collection.

plain_content:
Apache Kafka
Broker: Kafka cluster consists of brokers which are just nodes in the cluster hosting stateless server maintained by a zookeeper. 
Since there is no master-slave concept here, all brokers are peers. 
What is Zookeeper and Why is it needed in Kafka Cluster?
Zookeeper is a system for distributed cluster management. It is a distributed key-value store. It is highly-optimized for reads but writes are slower. It consists of an odd number of znodes known as an ensemble. In Kafka, it is needed for:
  *  Controller Election: All the read and writes from a partition for particular topics happen through the leader of the replica. Whenever the leader goes down, a new leader is elected by the zookeeper.
  *  Configuration of Topics: Metadata related to a topic that whether a particular topic is sitting in the broker, how many partitions are there, etc. are stored at the zookeeper end and are continuously in-sync whenever a message is produced.
  *  Access Control List(ACL) of a topic is maintained at a zookeeper.
Persistence: The message queue is maintained completely on a disk rather than keeping it in memory and several copies/replica called as ISR (in-sync replica)of the same data can be stored across different nodes. Hence, there is no chance of data loss due to failover scenarios and makes it durable.
Note: Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default and allows the user to implement at most once delivery by disabling retries on the producer and committing its offset prior to processing a batch of messages.
============================================
server.properties for Kafka Server
broker.id=101
listeners=PLAINTEXT:localhost:9091
logldirs=some_log_dir/kafka-logs-1
./bin/kafka-servert-start.sh ../config/server.properties
----------------------------------------
Creating a topic:
bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --zookeeper localhost:2181 --replication-factor 3 partitions 1 --topic topic1
Describing a particular topic:
bin/kafka-topics.sh --describe --zookeeper localhost:2181 --topic topic1
Deleting a topic:
bin/kafka-topics.sh --delete --zookeeper localhost:2181 --topic topic1
Note: Partition once set to a particular value cannot be decreased, it can only be increased.
----------------------------------------------
How Producer writes a message?
The Producer first fetches the Metadata of the topic in order to know which broker needs to be updated with the message.
Metadata is also stored at the brokers and is in continuous sync with the zookeeper because the zookeeper nodes are generally very less as compared to the no. of brokers.
So, many producers would like to connect to the zookeeper to access the metadata and the performance degrades.
Now, once the producer gets the metadata about the topic and partition, it writes the message in logs of the leader broker node and followers (ISR) copy it.
This writes operation can be either synchronous [i.e. the status about the message acknowledgment is returned to the producer only when the followers also copy that message in their log] 
or asynchronous [i.e. only the leader is updated with the new message, status is sent to the producer].
Retention Period: Messages on a disk can be persisted for a particular duration of time known as retention period, after that period automatic purging of the old messages will happen and will no longer be available for consumption. By default, it’s set to 7 days.
----------------------------------------------
The message can be written to a topic in three Strategies:
  *   send(key, value, topic, partition): specifically providing the partition in which writes needs to happen. This is not encouraged to use as it may create an imbalance in partition size.
  *  send(key, value, topic): Here, default HashPartitioner is used to determine the partition in which the message will be written by finding the hash of key and taking mod with no. of partition for that topic. Our own custom Partitioner can also be written.
  *   send(key=null, value, topic): In this case, the message is stored in all the partition in a round-robin fashion.
Creating a console producer:
bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --broker-list localhost:9091 --topic topic1
Changing retention period for a topic to 10sec:
bin/kafka-configs.sh --zookeeper localhost:2181 --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name topic1 --add-config retention.ms=10000
A producer can send the messages in the form of a batch to improve efficiency.
The consumer also retrieves the messages in the same way producer writes it by looking up into the metadata and reads the message from the leader partition. As Kafka is very fast and can get real-time messages, a single consumer will certainly have latency in reading a big chunk of a message from a topic known as consumer lag.
To overcome this problem, A Consumer group can be created which consists of several consumers having the same group id. Each consumer connects with a unique partition divided equally among all the consumers.
The assignment of the partition to a particular consumer is the responsibility of Group Coordinator — One of the brokers in the cluster is nominated for this role.
In order to manage the list of active consumers, all the consumer of a group sends their heartbeat to the group coordinator. 
The number of consumers in a group should be less than or equal to the number of partitions in that particular topic, violating the condition will end up in a situation where a consumer sits idle.
Creating a simple Consumer:
bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9091 --topic topic1
Creating consumer to read from particular offset and partition:
bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9091 --topic topic1 --offset 0 --partition 1
Creating a consumer group:
bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9091 --topic topic1 --group groupName
Multiple process/consumer of the above groupName can be created which is called Consumer Group.
More than one consumer can read a single topic at the same time.
Now, in order to remember till which offset the particular read, storage known as consumer offset as a hidden topic - __consumer_offsets is provided to store the last offset of a partition read by the consumer of a particular group.
The Consumer offset has the key as — > [Group Id, Topic, Partition] and value — > [Offset, …]
Consumer API:Similar to producer API, Kafka provides classes to connect to the bootstrap servers and get the messages. Deserializer needs to be written when passing a message of other than standard data types.
How Kafka is Fast?Kafka follows a certain strategy which is part of its design to make it perform better and faster.
  *  No Random Disk Access: It uses a sequential data structure known as an immutable queue where read and write operation is always constant time O(1). It appends the message at the end and read from the beginning or from a particular offset.
  *  Sequential I/O: Modern operating systems allocate most of their free memory to disk-caching and are faster for storing and retrieving sequential data.
  *  Zero Copy: The data from disk is unnecessarily loaded into the application memory as it is not being modified at all. So, instead of loading it to the application, it sends the same data from the kernel context buffer over the socket, NIC buffer and to the network.
  *  Batching of messages: Several messages are grouped together in order to avoid the multiple network call.
  *  Message Compression: Before transferring the message over the wire, it is compressed using compression algorithm like gzip, snappy, etc. and decompressed at the consumer API layer.
How the data reside on the Broker instance / physical disk?All the messages in a broker are stored in the log directory (log-dir-1) configured in the config file before turning the Kafka server up.
Inside that directory, a folder containing a partition of a particular topic can be found in the format as topic_name-partition_number
e.g. topic1–0. The __consumer_offsets topic is also stored in the same log directory.
Inside the partition directory of a particular topic, Kafka segment file 0000–00.log, index file 0000–00.index and time index 0000–00.timeindex can be found. All the data belonging to that partition are written in an active segment as a new segment file is created when the old segment size or time limit is reached. Indexes map each offset to their message’s position in the log. Since offset is sequential binary search is applied to find a data index in log file at a particular offset.
=======================================================================================
Kafka Topic Partitions
Kafka breaks topic logs up into partitions. A record is stored on a partition usually by record key if the key is present 
and round-robin if the key is missing (default behavior). 
The record key, by default, determines which partition a producer sends the record.
Offset Management
Kafka stores offset data in a topic called "__consumer_offset".
These topics use log compaction, which means they only save the most recent value per key.
When a consumer has processed data, it should commit offsets. If consumer process dies, it will be able to start up and start reading where it left off based on offset stored in "__consumer_offset"
What Can Kafka Consumers See?
What records can be consumed by a Kafka consumer? Consumers can’t read un-replicated data. Kafka consumers can only consume messages beyond the “High Watermark” offset of the partition. “Log end offset” is offset of the last record written to log partition and where producers writes to next.
“High Watermark” is the offset of the last record that was successfully replicated to all partition’s followers. Consumer only reads up to the “High Watermark”.
Consumer to Partition Cardinality 
Only a single consumer from the same consumer group can access a single partition.
If consumer group count exceeds the partition count, then the extra consumers remain idle.
Kafka can use the idle consumers for failover. If there are more partitions than consumer group, then some consumers will read from more than one partition.
In same consumer group a partition can be consumed by only one consumer, if partitions are more than no. of consumers in a group then multiple partitions can be consumed by one consumer. partitions are shared accross consumer groups..
Multi-Threaded Kafka ConsumersYou can run more than one Consumer in a JVM process by using threads.
Does each consumer group have its own offset?
Yes. The consumer groups have their own offset for every partition in the topic which is unique to what other consumer groups have.
When can a consumer see a record?
A consumer can see a record after the record gets fully replicated to all followers.
What happens if there are more consumers than partitions?
The extra consumers remain idle until another consumer dies.

What is message ordering :
  *  If key= null, data is send in round robin
  *  If key is sent, then all message for that key will always go to same partition. This can be used to order the messages for a specific key since order is guaranteed in same partition.
===================
Kafka topics are divided into a number of partitions.
 Any record written to a particular topic goes to particular partition. Each record is assigned and 
 identified by an unique offset. Replication is implemented at partition level. 
 The redundant unit of topic partition is called replica. The logic that decides partition for a message is configurable. 
 Partition helps in reading/writing data in parallel by splitting in different partitions spread over multiple brokers.
 Each replica has one server acting as leader and others as followers. Leader handles the read/write while followers replicate
 the data. In case leader fails, any one of the followers is elected as the leader.
======================
Rebalancing
As a consumer group scales up and down, the running consumers split the partitions up amongst themselves.
Rebalancing is triggered by a shift in ownership between a partition and consumer which could be caused by the crash of a consumer or broker or the addition of a topic or partition. It allows for safe addition or removal of consumer from the system.
On start up, a broker is marked as the coordinator for the subset of consumer groups which receive the RegisterConsumer Request from consumers and returns the RegisterConsumer Response containing the list of partitions they should own.
The coordinator also starts failure detection to check if the consumers are alive or dead. When the consumer fails to send a heartbeat to the coordinator broker before the session timeout, the coordinator marks the consumer as dead and a rebalance is set in place to occur.
This session time period can be set using the session.timeout.ms property of the Kafka service.
The heartbeat.interval.ms property makes healthy consumers aware of the occurrence of a rebalance so as to re-send RegisterConsumer requests to the coordinator.
=============
brokers will continue to be heavily depend on Zookeeper for:
  *  Server failure detection.
  *  Data partitioning.
  *  In-sync data replication.
  *  zookeeper elects controller among available brokers which is responsible for assigning broker of some specific partition leader
But nowadays its usage is limited and kafka project will remove its dependency soon..
Electing a controller. The controller is one of the brokers and is responsible for maintaining the leader/follower relationship for all the partitions. When a node shuts down, it is the controller that tells other replicas to become partition leaders to replace the partition leaders on the node that is going away. Zookeeper is used to elect a controller, make sure there is only one and elect a new one it if it crashes.
Cluster membership - which brokers are alive and part of the cluster? this is also managed through ZooKeeper.
Topic configuration - which topics exist, how many partitions each has, where are the replicas, who is the preferred leader, what configuration overrides are set for each topic
 Quotas - how much data is each client allowed to read and write
ACLs - who is allowed to read and write to which topic (old high level consumer) - Which consumer groups exist, who are their members and what is the latest offset each group got from each partition.
Kafka stores basic metadata in Zookeeper such as information about topics, brokers, consumer offsets (queue readers)
Once the Zookeeper quorum is down, brokers could result in a bad state and could not normally serve client requests, etc. Although when Zookeeper quorum recovers, the Kafka brokers should be able to resume to normal state automatically, there are still a few corner cases the they cannot and a hard kill-and-recovery is required to bring it back to normal. Hence it is recommended to closely monitor your zookeeper cluster and provision it so that it is performant.

>> only 1.

>> consumer groups can read simultaniouly from partitions but within each group only one consumer can read from a single partition
what if one consumer reads from 1 partition from and another consumer is reading same replicated partition abd belongs to 2nd consumer group
>> replicated partitions just sits idle , you can only read from master / leader partition
how these consumer offsets are managed accross the brokers ??
>> kafka and zookeers both maintain it.

2) Security Reasons: As string is used in urls , db connection urls and others, immutability makes these safe

Design Patterns
Design Patterns : Its best practice for common problems.
Given in book : Gangs of Four
Types:
Creational : About how objects are created
Structural : About adding / composing abject inside another object
Behavioural : About how objects will interact with each other
Factory Pattern:
Just have one method to create objects of one family.
eg. Hibernate : SessionFactory.openSession()
Java: Calendar.getInstance(), Integer.valueOf()
Abstract Factory :
It have multiple methods to create object of multiple family types without specifying concrete type.
  *  Abstract factory have multiple methods to create different configuration / composition of same type
  *  or it can have multiple methods to create different types with different compositions
Its similar to Factory but its Factory of Factories.
Now similar thing can also be done using multiple factories but we can incorrectly mix them to create a composite object
so abstract factory also takes care of correct configurations.
eg. a mac os window can only have mac os style buttons it can't have windows style buttons, 
and if we use multiple separate factories one for mac window, mac button, windows window, windows button then we can incorrectly mix
them to create logically invalid composite object so instead we can use abstract factory to not just to take care the creation of object
but also valid configurations.
eg.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
==================================================================================================
Observer Pattern:
Tomcat: ServletContextListener : contextInitialized, contextDestroyed
==================================================================================================
Builder Pattern:
Solves issue of creating object with large no. of parameters
StringBuilder's append() method.
Mongo: Document's append() method
===================================================================================================
Prototype Pattern:
Its used to create object by cloning.
===================================================================================================
Decorator Pattern:
Take object & wrap it with our own additional functionality.
eg. new BufferedReader( new FileReader(..))
Dynamic proxies are often used to implement decorators. One example of this is AOP in Spring.
Proxy vs Decorator:
Decorator Pattern focuses on dynamically adding functions to an object,
while Proxy Pattern focuses on controlling access to an object.
 
=================================================================================================
Mediator Design Pattern:
Mediator works as router between objects.
eg. Air Traffic control mediator for flights.
Java concurrency : Executor's execute() method.
====================================================================================================
Chain of Responsibility Pattern:
Its used to loose couple in software design, a request from client is passed to chain of objects to process them.
Then if any object can handle it or pass it on to the next.
Logger -> log() method
Eg.
Request class is just a pojo that holds data
Now there is abstract class for all objects which can process & this abstract class has ref. who will try to handle next.
Now create concrete class of this abstract class so that we can create multiple processing classes
Now create class that creates chain and issues command to chain
Now issue commands, Command objects in chain either handle themselves or by using parent abstract class forwards this to next
in chain object until next is null.
==================================================================================================
Iterator Pattern:
Iterator hides actual implementation of traversal through the collection & client program just uses iterator methods.
So Iterator abstracts internal collection traversal and show provides simple way to client to iterate over all objects by just
checking whether there are any objects left and if left then give me one
( so client doesn't knows collection structure and anything else.. just give me next object.. )
eg. Java collection traversal.
===================================================================================================
Singleton : create only single object and return that only whenever someone asks for it.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21604243/correct-implementation-of-initialization-on-demand-holder-idiom
More Full proof :
public class Singleton {
   ...
   private static class LazyHolder {
       static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton();
   }
   public static Singleton getInstance() {
       return LazyHolder.INSTANCE;
   }
}
============================================================================================
Strategy Design Pattern : 
Based on composition.
Provides you the flexibility to change the behaviour of object at runtime.
Less coupling between the client code and the solution/algorithm code.
Identification: Strategy pattern can be recognised by a method that lets nested object do the actual work, as well as the setter that allows replacing that object with a different one.
Examples:
Collections.sort() -> uses Comparable , Comparator provided
Collections.binarySearch(..)
Steps:
1) Define strategy interface
Define classes that implements strategy
Define class that uses plugin strategy
2) Use class, inject / change strategy at runtime
Strategy vs Factory :
Factory is about creating objects while Strategy is about plugging behaviour or delegating behaviour at runtime ( by polymorphism )
=====================================================================================================
Template Method Design Pattern:
Steps:
1) Define abstract class with common behaviour and variables,
define all methods that needs to be implemented by child class abstract
and concrete template method which controls the execution flow of these methods, its like steps,
so template method only controls common steps sequence, rest all is delegated to concrete implementation.
2) Define concrete class implementing all abstract methods from Template
3) Create appropriate concrete class object of Template and execute template method.
=================================================================================================
Adaptor pattern :
Adaptor use to make incompatible interfaces ( not necessarily interface only ) interoperable with each other
Think like Electric Adaptor which makes US plug interoperable with UK socket.
examples:
java.util.Collections.list() : Converts Any collection to List using Enumerator
java.io.InputStreamReader(InputStream) : converts InputStream to Reader
marshal() and unmarshal() methods of XML /JSON to POJO converter
Steps:
1) Functionality of Rowing Boat and Fishing Boat is very much different
2) Captain can only handle Rowing Boat
2) So we create adaptor for him to use Fishing Boat

The x in INT(x) has nothing to do with space requirements or any other performance issues,
 it's really just the display width. Generally setting the display widths to a reasonable value 
 is mostly useful with the UNSIGNED ZEROFILL option.

//INT(4) UNSIGNED ZEROFILL
0001
0002 

so int(x) will have same space as int, x denotes only how many places to show..

=========================================

MySQL

a varchar(16) is no different disk-wise than a varchar(128) but
access wise it makes a huge difference, since when MySql creates the result set in memory 
it turns it into a matrix, thus if your largest field is 16 characters,
 but the field is defined as 128 characters you have to allocate an extra 112 characters for every row.
 This wastes a lot a memory.

 Not only do you have to allocate an extra 112 characters for each row in memory, 
 but you will have a great deal more L1 cache misses when each row is iterated over.
 This is compared to a VARCHAR(16) column type, where you could squeeze a lot more rows with this column 
 into high-speed cache under-the-hood.

=====================================

MongoDB Sparse vs Partial Index 

Sparse index is optimized index which only contains pointers to documents that has value(s) in the indexed fields. For example you would like to add index on lastname field

{ _id: 1, firstname: 'John', lastname: 'Black', age: 20 }
{ _id: 2, firstname: 'Stive', lastname: 'White', age: 17 }
{ _id: 3, firstname: 'Tom', age: 22 }
if you run

db.users.createIndex({ lastname: 1 });
command, it will add indexes on 3 documents, but you don't need to have index on document where is no lastname value (_id: 3). It waste of space and memory. To avoid empty fields' indexing, mongodb has sparse index, which is simply check for non empty value. So when you add sparse: true

db.users.createIndex({ lastname: 1, sparse: true });
Mongodb will add indexes only for 2 documents (_id: 1, _id:2). Its great, but what to do if you want to index only those users' documents which are older than 18 years? You cant use sparse index because it only checks documents for value existence.

This is why partial indexes were created.

db.person.createIndex( 
 { age: 1}, 
 { partialFilterExpression: { age: { $gte: 18 }, lastname: { $exists: true }}
);
This example will put index only for 1 document(id: 1). Partial index is complex version of sparse, it will filter documents not only checking their existence, but using conditions provided in partialFilterExpression field.

"},{"insert":"$where:","attributes":{"bold":true}},{"insert":"

In general, you should use $where only when you can’t express your query using another operator.

Use the $where operator to pass either a string containing a JavaScript expression 
or a full JavaScript function to the query system. The $where provides greater flexibility,
 but requires that the database processes the JavaScript expression or function for 
 each document in the collection. Reference the document in the JavaScript expression 
 or function using either this or obj .

Limitations:

$where evaluates JavaScript and cannot take advantage of indexes. Therefore, 
query performance improves when you express your query using the standard MongoDB operators

db.myCollection.find( { $where: "this.credits == this.debits" } );
db.myCollection.find( { $where: "obj.credits == obj.debits" } );

db.myCollection.find( { $where: function() { return (this.credits == this.debits) } } );
db.myCollection.find( { $where: function() { return obj.credits == obj.debits; } } );

"},{"insert":"Journaling","attributes":{"bold":true}},{"insert":"
MongoDB uses memory mapped files and flushes to disk are done every 60 seconds, 
which means you can lose a maximum of 60 seconds + the flush time worth of data.

To reduce the chance of losing data, MongoDB added journaling -since 2.0 it’s been enabled by default.
 Journaling records changes to the database to disk every 100ms. If the database is shutdown unexpectedly,
 this will be replayed before starting up to make sure the database is in a consistent state.
 This is the nearest thing in MongoDB to a commit in a more traditional database.

Advantages of MongoDB over MySQL :
1) flexible schema so just change code and its done , while in case of mysql alter table which may take time if many writes happening.
2) replications options like how many replica's should ack for doc is there in mongodb so more fine grained control
while replications is hidden thing in mysql we can't specify dynamically per row..
3) MongoDB have Sharding and Replication built in, while in MySQL its separate plugin.
Disadvantage:
1) No relation between collections
2) No transaction support ( its in newer MongoDB v4 )

every object / doc in mongodb represented by objectID stored in _id field

Array Element Find:
The following example queries for all documents where the field tags value
is an array with exactly two elements, "red" and "blank", in the specified order

NOT THE SOLUTION :JUST MATHCES ARRAY WITH EXACTLY 2 ELEMENTS IN SAME ORDER

If, instead, you wish to find an array that contains

db.inventory.find( { tags: { $all: ["red", "blank"] } } )

ordered	boolean	Optional arg, if not specified Defaults to true
If true, perform an ordered insert of the documents in the array, 
and if an error occurs with one of documents, MongoDB will return 
without processing the remaining documents in the array.
If false, perform an unordered insert, and if an error occurs with one of documents,

Evaluation Query OPerator:
$where:
In general, you should use $where only when you can’t express your query using another operator.
Use the $where operator to pass either a string containing a JavaScript expression 
or a full JavaScript function to the query system. The $where provides greater flexibility,
 but requires that the database processes the JavaScript expression or function for 
 each document in the collection. Reference the document in the JavaScript expression 
 or function using either this or obj .
Limitations:
$where evaluates JavaScript and cannot take advantage of indexes. Therefore, 
query performance improves when you express your query using the standard MongoDB operators
db.myCollection.find( { $where: "this.credits == this.debits" } );
db.myCollection.find( { $where: "obj.credits == obj.debits" } );
db.myCollection.find( { $where: function() { return (this.credits == this.debits) } } );
db.myCollection.find( { $where: function() { return obj.credits == obj.debits; } } );

In the context of scaling MongoDB:
REPLICATION creates additional copies of the data and allows for automatic failover to another node. 
Replication may help with horizontal scaling of reads if you are OK to read data that potentially isn't the latest.
SHARDING allows for horizontal scaling of data writes by partitioning data across multiple servers using a shard key.
 It's important to choose a good shard key. For example, a poor choice of shard key could lead to "hot spots" 
 of data only being written on a single shard.

to interleave with its update of the matched documents.

Journaling
MongoDB uses memory mapped files and flushes to disk are done every 60 seconds, 
which means you can lose a maximum of 60 seconds + the flush time worth of data.
To reduce the chance of losing data, MongoDB added journaling -since 2.0 it’s been enabled by default.
 Journaling records changes to the database to disk every 100ms. If the database is shutdown unexpectedly,
 this will be replayed before starting up to make sure the database is in a consistent state.
 This is the nearest thing in MongoDB to a commit in a more traditional database.

Timestamp − ctimestamp. This can be handy for recording when a document has been modified or added.
Object − This datatype is used for embedded documents.
Null − This type is used to store a Null value.
Symbol − This datatype is used identically to a string; however, it's generally reserved for languages that use a specific symbol type.
Date − This datatype is used to store the current date or time in UNIX time format. You can specify your own date time by creating object of Date and passing day, month, year into it.
Object ID − This datatype is used to store the document’s ID.
Binary data − This datatype is used to store binary data.
Code − This datatype is used to store JavaScript code into the document.

{"ops":[{"insert":"Redis : a distributed shared cache

Replication :

Replication involves a master server which serves reads and writes, 
and duplicates all data to one or more slave servers (which serves reads but not writes). 
Slaves can be used to replace a master in case of failure, spread read request load, or to perform backups 
of the database to reduce load on the master.

--------------------------------

Cluster:

Clusters are used when you have more data than RAM in a single machine: 
the data is automatically split (based on the key) across multiple databases, 
increasing the amount of data you can store. Clients requesting a key from any cluster node 
will be redirected to the node holding the key, and are expected to learn the locations of keys 
to reduce the number of redirects.

-------------------------------

Replicaton + Cluster: 

Redis Cluster supports replication by adding slaves to existing nodes, 
if a master becomes unreachable then its slave will be promoted to master.

Sentinel
Last but not least, Redis Sentinel can be used to manage replicated servers 
(not clustered, see below.) Clients connect to a Sentinel and request a master or slave to communicate with,
 the sentinels handle health checks of the masters/slaves, and will automatically promote a slave 
 if a master is unreachable. You need to have at least 3 sentinels running so that they can agree on reachability of nodes, 
 and to ensure the sentinels aren’t a single point of failure.

Cluster handles its own promotion and does not need Sentinel in front of it.

-----------------------------

The quorum value is the number of Sentinels that need to agree about the fact the master is not reachable.
 However the quorum is only used to detect the failure. In order to actually perform a failover,
 one of the Sentinels need to be elected leader for the failover and be authorized to proceed.
 This only happens with the vote of the majority of the Sentinel processes.

---------------------------------

Redis can handle up to 2 ³² keys, and was tested in practice to handle at least 250 million keys per instance.

An empty instance uses ~ 3MB of memory.

1 Million small Keys -> String Value pairs use ~ 85MB of memory.

1 Million Keys -> Hash value, representing an object with 5 fields, use ~ 160 MB of memory.

Redis is single threaded. How can I exploit multiple CPU / cores?
It’s not very frequent that CPU becomes your bottleneck with Redis, as usually Redis is either memory or network bound.
 If it is the case, horizontal or vertical scaling of Redis instances will help to reduce CPU related bottlenecks.
Redis is an in-memory but persistent on disk database.
Redis Persistence -> RDB : point-in-time snapshots of your dataset at specified intervals. (Data backup)
| AOF : logs every write operation received by the server. (More Durable)

=================================================================
"}]}

plain_content:
Spring AOP
So to enable Aspect support just add spring-boot-aop-starter
and annotate the class containing aspects with @Aspect, there is no annotation on target classes or methods on which these aspects gets applied so aspects are completely independent/non-interfering and targets are not aware of their existance..
Terminology:
Aspect :  its a simple class with @Aspect annotation which implements cross cutting concerns ( eg. transaction , logging.. )
Advise : Its action taken be Aspect when some condition ie method execution matches..
  *  @Before: runs before method execution
  *  @After : runs after mothod execution , irr-respective of method's successful execution ( runs even if there is some error or exception.. )
  *  @AfterReturning: runs after method execution but only if execution is successful ( it it throws any checked or unchecked exception then this will not run)
  *  @Around: Runs before and after method execution.. even can cancel method execution
  *  @AfterThrowing: runs after method has thrown some exception
Joinpoint : An application has thousands of methods these are joinpoints as currently in Spring AOP we can only advise methods, so joinpoint is a thing on which we can apply advise.
Pointcut : As its not feasible to apply advise on every joinpoint so we use some expression / string to specify where to apply advise, that expression/string is pointcut.
Weaving : Its a process of linking Aspect with target object ( i.e object that is being advised.. ), its maybe compile time or runtime, Spring AOP is runtime.
if we want just args to be logged then @Before is ok, but if we want parameters & return type also need to be logged then 
@AfterReturning ( if we only want to work if method returns successfully ) or @After ( gets executed even if there is some issue with method ) is required.
AOP is implemented as Interceptor, so all Advises are Interceptors of MethodInterceptor parent type.
AOP Advantages:
Cleaner Code : As we write AOP separately code gets cleaner.
Centralised Cross cutting concerns code : as code is at one place its easy to maintain
AOP Limitations :
1) Only public methods can be advised ( no private protected default.. )
2) Auto wiring or dependency injection doesn't work directly as spring doesn't proxy this object.. 
( @Configurable annotation on aspect class makes it work.. Marks a class as being eligible for Spring-driven configuration )
3) Direct method calls in target object ( an object which is being advised.. ) from other methods don't trigger advises as they are not going through proxy

have @Transactional applied to it, but this is not we want, so always specify @Transactional on service
Some JPARepo methods return Optional use those methods, some methods will silently try to do operation and on failure will
do nothing ie. No Exception, while some methods on error throw DataAccessException's which are runtime wrapper exceptions. And by Default @Transactional is only rollbacks for Any RuntimeException only.
delete() vs deleteById() :

@Validated is used to validate path and request params of Spring controller params.
@Valid vs @Validated : @Valid validates whole objects with all nested objects, while @Validated is for partial validation
i.e we can group various things and validate specific groups only.
@Transactional :
When does transaction is commited ? well every method that is marked with @Transaction if it doesn't throw any RuntimeException then after method returns transaction is committed.
Default is If transaction is not started then start new it else continue existing transaction. after returning from method its commited. Now as Every SQLException is wrapped in DataAccessException which is runtime so if any sql exception
happens then transaction is rollbacked, optionally we can specify on which other types of Exceptions a transaction
should be rollbacked.
All @Transactional behaviour is implemented as AOP.
And lets say we want 2 @Transactional methods to be clubbed in one transaction then we must create a transaction
before calling those methods so these methods with default @Transactional annotation will use that existing transaction.
Eg.
Propagation property of @Transactional states that when to create a new transaction.
mandatory : txn must be present before calling this method else exception
never : shouldn't be run in txn else exception
required: if txn is there then use that else create new
requires_new : suspend existing txn , create new txn and use that for this method only

You can generally trust Spring to do the right thing. It detects configuration problems,
such as references to non-existent beans and circular dependencies, at container load-time.
 Spring sets properties and resolves dependencies as late as possible, when the bean is actually created.
 This means that a Spring container which has loaded correctly can later generate an exception
 when you request an object if there is a problem creating that object or one of its dependencies.
 For example, the bean throws an exception as a result of a missing or invalid property.
 This potentially delayed visibility of some configuration issues is why ApplicationContext implementations by default
 pre-instantiate singleton beans. At the cost of some upfront time and memory to create these beans
 before they are actually needed, you discover configuration issues when the ApplicationContext is created,
 not later. You can still override this default behavior so that singleton beans will lazy-initialize,
 rather than be pre-instantiated.

 ====================================================================================

Beans which are dependencies of others gets configured first before those beans who defines those as dependencies

========================================================================================

In contrast to the other scopes, Spring does not manage the complete lifecycle of a prototype bean:
 the container instantiates, configures, and otherwise assembles a prototype object,
 and hands it to the client, with no further record of that prototype instance.
 Thus, although initialization lifecycle callback methods are called on all objects regardless of scope,
 in the case of prototypes, configured destruction lifecycle callbacks are not called.
 The client code must clean up prototype-scoped objects and release expensive resources that the prototype bean(s)
 are holding. To get the Spring container to release resources held by prototype-scoped beans,
 try using a custom bean post-processor, which holds a reference to beans that need to be cleaned up.

not even within @Configuration classes (see above). This is due to technical limitations:

Spring MVC type conversion : PropertyEditor or Converter?

I am looking for the easiest and simplest way to bind and convert data in Spring MVC.
If possible, without doing any xml configuration.

So far I've been using PropertyEditors like so :

public class CategoryEditor extends PropertyEditorSupport {

   // Converts a String to a Category (when submitting form)
   @Override
   public void setAsText(String text) {
       Category c = new Category(text);
       this.setValue(c);
   }

   // Converts a Category to a String (when displaying form)
   @Override
   public String getAsText() {
       Category c = (Category) this.getValue();
       return c.getName();
   }

}
and

...
public class MyController {

   @InitBinder
   public void initBinder(WebDataBinder binder) {
       binder.registerCustomEditor(Category.class, new CategoryEditor());
   }

   ...

}

It is simple : both conversion are defined in the same class, and the binding is straightforward.
 If I wanted to do a general binding across all my controllers, I could still add 3 lines in my xml config.

But Spring 3.x introduced a new way to do it, using Converters :

Within a Spring container, this system can be used as an alternative to PropertyEditors

So let's say I want to use Converters because it is "the latest alternative". I would have to create two converters :

public class StringToCategory implements Converter<String, Category> {

   @Override
   public Category convert(String source) {
       Category c = new Category(source);
       return c;
   }

}

public class CategoryToString implements Converter<Category, String> {

   @Override
   public String convert(Category source) {
       return source.getName();
   }

}
First drawback : I have to make two classes. Benefit : no need to cast thanks to genericity.

Then, how do I simply data bind the converters ?

Second drawback : I haven't found any simple way (annotations or other programmatic facilities)
to do it in a controller : nothing like someSpringObject.registerCustomConverter(...);.

The only ways I've found would be tedious, not simple, and only about general cross-controller binding :

Java config (only in Spring 3.1+) :

@EnableWebMvc
@Configuration
public class WebConfig extends WebMvcConfigurerAdapter {

   @Override
   protected void addFormatters(FormatterRegistry registry) {
       registry.addConverter(new StringToCategory());
       registry.addConverter(new CategoryToString());
   }

}

In my mind, PropertyEditors are limited in scope - they help convert String to a type, and this string typically comes
 from UI, and so registering a PropertyEditor using @InitBinder and using WebDataBinder makes sense.

Converter on the other hand is more generic, it is intended for ANY conversion in the system -
not just for UI related conversions(String to target type).
For eg, Spring Integration uses a converter extensively for converting a message payload to a desired type.

${...} is the property placeholder syntax. It can only be used to dereference properties.

#{...} is SpEL syntax, which is far more capable and complex. It can also handle property placeholders, and a lot more besides.

Both are valid, and neither is deprecated.

${expr} --> Immediate Evaluation

#{expr} --> Deferred Evaluation

Immediate evaluation means that the expression is evaluated and the result returned as soon as the page is first rendered. Deferred evaluation means that the technology using the expression language can use its own machinery to evaluate the expression sometime later during the page’s lifecycle, whenever it is appropriate to do so.

Does orphanRemoval need to be set to true in order to support removing elements from a collection?

@ElementCollection field implicitly has Cascasde.ALL + orphanRemoval = true

Cascading Remove

Marking a reference field with CascadeType.REMOVE (or CascadeType.ALL, which includes REMOVE) indicates that remove operations should be cascaded automatically to entity objects that are referenced by that field (multiple entity objects can be referenced by a collection field):

@Entity
class Employee {
    :
   @OneToOne(cascade=CascadeType.REMOVE)
   private Address address;
    :
}
Orphan Removal

JPA 2 supports an additional and more aggressive remove cascading mode which can be specified using the orphanRemoval element of the @OneToOne and @OneToMany annotations:

@Entity
class Employee {
    :
   @OneToOne(orphanRemoval=true)
   private Address address;
    :
}
DIFFERENCE:-

The difference between the two settings is in the response to disconnecting a relationship. For example, such as when setting the address field to null or to another Address object.

If orphanRemoval=true is specified the disconnected Address instance is automatically removed. This is useful for cleaning up dependent objects (e.g. Address) that should not exist without a reference from an owner object (e.g. Employee).
If only cascade=CascadeType.REMOVE is specified no automatic action is taken since disconnecting a relationship is not a remove
operation.

---------------------

An easy way to understand the difference between CascadeType.REMOVE and orphanRemoval=true.

For orphan removal: If you invoke setOrders(null), the related Order entities will be removed in db automatically.

For remove cascade: If you invoke setOrders(null), the related Order entities will NOT be removed in db automatically.

When do you need @ResponseStatus annotation in Spring MVC? (answer)

This is a good question for 3 to 5 years as an experienced Spring developer. The @ResponseStatus annotation is required during error handling in Spring MVC and REST. Normally, when an error or exception is thrown at the server side, the web server returns a blanket HTTP status code 500 — Internal server error.

This may work for a human user but not for REST clients. You need to send them the proper status code, like 404, if the resource is not found. That's where you can use the @ResponseStatus annotation, which allows you to send custom HTTP status codes along with proper error message in case of an exception.

In order to use it, you can create custom exceptions and annotate them using the @ResponseStatus annotation and proper HTTP status code and reason.

When such exceptions are thrown from the controller's handler methods and not handled anywhere else, then the appropriate HTTP response with the proper HTTP status code is sent to the client.

For example, if you are writing a RESTful web service for a library that provides book information, then you can use @ResponseStatus to create an exception that returns the HTTP response code 404 when a book is not found instead of the Internal Server Error (500), as shown below:

@ResponseStatus(value=HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, reason="No such Book") // 404
 public class BookNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    // ...
 }

How Tomcat accepts connection? and whats overall behaviour for Request,Responses

( newer tomcat uses NonBlocking IO so this accept count , max no of connections doesn't matter that much anymore.. )

You would have to tune it according to your environment.

Sometimes it's more useful to increase the size of the backlog (acceptCount) instead of the maximum number of threads.

Say, instead of

<Connector ... maxThreads="500" acceptCount="50"

you use

<Connector ... maxThreads="300" acceptCount="150"

you can get much better performance in some cases, cause there would be less threads disputing the resources 
and the backlog queue would be consumed faster.


maxConnections When this number has been reached, the server will accept, but not process,
 one further connection. once the limit has been reached, the operating system may still accept connections based 
 on the acceptCount setting. (The maximum queue length for incoming connection requests when all possible reques
 t processing threads are in use. Any requests received when the queue is full will be refused. The default value is 100.)
 
 
maxThreads
The maximum number of request processing threads to be created by this Connector,
 which therefore determines the maximum number of simultaneous requests that can be handled.
 If not specified, this attribute is set to 200. If an executor is associated with this connector,
 this attribute is ignored as the connector will execute tasks using the executor rather than an internal thread pool.

Hibernate With MySQL
Hibernate Properties in Spring Data JPA:
Now @Entity must be there to mark this pojo.
@Id must there and it must be wrapper type variable ( or any serializable type )
@GeneratedValue must be there else Hibernate doesn't know how to generate this id. ( else we have to assign id manually before calling save() )
Now If we dont specify what GeneratedValue type needs to be used then Hibernate generates new table called hibernate_sequence.
hibernate_sequence table shows next value to be assigned in coming insert.
So when we say GenerationType.AUTO -> defaults to GenerationType.TABLE in MySQL
Hibernate picks the TABLE generator instead of IDENTITY when the underlying database does not support sequences.
Now if we use SEQUENCE, hibernate doesn't throw error that MySQL dont support this.. it uses hibernate_sequence. ( so for MySQL GenerationType.TABLE & GenerationType.SEQUENCE are same or their effect is same)
So MySQL have AUTO_INCREMENT functionality, we can use GenerationType.IDENTITY here
( always use spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop while playing with table designs else hibernate may behave erratic )
( here default can be only used in Annotation method's default value, can't use in class or interface only Annotation interface )
optionally we can override table's name by specifying name attribute or can use @Table(name="emp"), default it create table as same name from Class Name.
Now ideally we should use either GenerationType.SEQUENCE or GenerationType.IDENTITY, GenerationType.TABLE should be only used if no other option.

so Entity with UserStage is written as DB table with name user_stage
accountExpires -> account_expires

@Embeddable specifies this content of this whole class should be added as columns in Entity which owns this or has this variable defined.
Now how to use this composite primary key as foreign key in other tables

@Column : We can override column name with this default is variable name, i.e whatever variable name is that same is used as column name at the time of table creation. We can also specify whether this column can be nullable , max length, uniqueness , updatable or not, can this column considered in insert statement i.e insertable.

Hibernate Types:
1) Entity Types : These have db identity
2) Value Types: These dont have separate DB identity they are part of Entity types.
  *  Basic : eg. String, int, datetime
  *  Composite Type: eg. Address
  *  Collection
Composite Types ( has a ): Its a group of values in Java class, these are embedded as a part of owning entity ( so no separate table for these.. ), so this gets added as various columns in owning entity table.
Collection Types: These can have Basic or Composite value types, these gets stored in separate table.

@Embeddable & @Embedded

 Notice this Address class dont have @Id column

String) while @OneToMany is used to map entities, and as this is kind of one to many, and collection table is at many side so this table has foreign key columns that map back to owning collection primary key, works on only List & Set directly, for map we need another annotation,@CollectionTable can be used to override table name and other attributes for List,Set,Map )
This is used to persist collections. It gets persisted in separate table. uses primary key of owning collection as its columns so that we can query it.
If we want to modify name of collection table or columns in it.. then use @CollectionTable , no of columns should be exactly equal to no of primary key columns eg. in below example there is composite primary key of 2 columns so we must specify 2 join columns else error.

Entity Associations 
(cascade type must be specified in owning entity else exception in Spring data JPA case,
also always add mappedBy in non association owning entity to tell Hibernate which entity has Fkey, else weird schema )
Types : OneToOne, OneToMany, ManyToOne, ManyToMany
Direction : UniDirectional ( only owning entity has variable of other entity ), BiDirectional ( both entities have variables pointing to each other)
Now owner of association is the one who has Fkey in its table, its different owning entity.
@JoinColumn is always defined on owner of association table, so this is used to define Fkey or rename or override attributes of Fkey
OneToOne Unidirectional
Now we just mapped @OneToOne Unidirectional relationship but this doesn't save non owning entity,In this case Biodata is non owning entity. So we must specify hibernate to save other entity i.e Biodata object too whenever we save Employee object.
Optionally @JoinColumn can be used to specify Fkey column name ( default is {tablename}_{pkey name} eg biodata_id )
@JoinColumn represents Fkey, so when we specify it we define Fkey. ( so new Fkey column gets added )
@JoinColumn must be specified in one entity only, if we specify in both entities then circular dependency happens.
Optionally we can also specify which column in other entity ( non owning ) this Fkey references
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Other Attributes on OneToOne and other mapping annotations ( like OneToMany, ManyToOne.. )
CascadeType : This is to specify when any operation happens on owning entity what should happen to other entity.
So ideally we should use ALL.
Detach : when parent ( i.e owning entity ) gets detached child also get detached
Merge: When parent gets updated, child too
Persist: when parent gets inserted child too
Refresh: when parent gets refreshed i.e reloaded from DB child too
Remove: when parent gets deleted child too
So if we don't use CascadeType.ALL then at the time of inserting parent entity, as we told hibernate to not save child entity.. it can't insert parent also, as parent references child.. so we must manually insert child and set persisted object back in parent, only after that parent can be saved..
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
FetchType.LAZY or EAGER
Eager: load child object as soon as possible
Lazy : load child object only when its is going to be accessed
( if object is detached then this throws Lazy Initialization exception.. )
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
optional = true ( default ) / false
whether child entity is optional or nullable or not
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OrphanRemoval : true / false ( default ) ( useful when we want to set child entity null.. or only remove child entity, so that it can be deleted from its table.. ) ( so we should ideally use this always as true.. )
when we remove parent object child object also gets removed if we use CascadeType.ALL or CascadeType.REMOVE.
But if we want to remove only child object then what to do?? So if we just set child variable as null in parent.. as this is not a remove operation
CascadeType doesn't works here and only in parent table null set in Fkey but child row still exists in child table.
So when we set OrphanRemoval to true & set child as null , child entity gets deleted automatically.
eg
Before OrphanRemoval : false
child table row is still there even if we set it null in parent.

But this doesn't work as Jackson ( default parser in spring boot ) doesn't know how to construct polymorphic types i.e how to parse generic json to specific type. So we use extra annotations to do that.

	so saving will work like this but dont know how delete, update will work via JPA.

Now this @type in json is for Jackson to create & parse appropriate object, but hibernate keeps track which row is which class's object by using auto generated dtype column its default value is class name. we can override this by using @DiscriminatorValue on each entity class
Now we can't use Inheritance as parent type as in Inheritance variable is implicitly final i.e it must be assigned at declaration time. so we can't use setters and even if we use @Access(AccessType.FIELD) we can't change final variables..

Disadvantages: 
1) All tables share one primary key. GenerationType.Identity is not supported so we must either use Sequence or Table.
2) Slow performance because of UNION ALL from all tables.

i.e in this case if we insert 2wheeler type then data gets inserted only in 2wheeler table, no entry in parent table..
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4) Joined Table (shares Pkey from parent, left join is used to get data, parent and child tables get created and each one of them hold its own data eg. so for insert there will be 2 inserts, one in parent and other one will be in child table):
Tables share one Pkey and child table only have its own columns so partial data. At the time of retrieval join is done on parent and specific child table.
eg.
So for insert there will be 2 inserts , one in parent and other will be specific child table

Hibernate 2nd Level Cache ( distributed cache ):
1) Collections need to be marked @Cachable explicitly, By default they are not cached.
2) Default key for cached entity is {fully qualified class name}#{Pkey}
