Hibernate Pitfalls:
1) Must use mappedBy else weird schema :
eg.
@Entity
public class Customer
{
@ManyToMany
Collection<Address> addr;
}
@Entity
public class Address
{
@ManyToMany
Collection<Customer> custs;
}
In this we expect hibernate to create one joining table but it creates 2, Customer_Address & Address_Customer. So we must specify mappedBy in Any one entity to crate only one Joining table.
2) Default @OneToMany uses JoinTable so If we want Fkey based then must use @JoinColumn as many side entity
3) No Ordering :
@OneToMany
List<Products> prod;
Here Hibernate uses Bag not list, its own internal collection ( Hibernate uses its own internal collections, no matter what you specify in entity class,even if you specify @OneToMany List<Product> prod = new ArrayList<>(); As every entity gets proxied , that proxy class will use hibernate's internal collections.. for getting data..)
4) If we add / remove element from collection, hibernate removes all rows from of that collection from table and inserts updated collection.
5) As we can specify Lazy Loading in Hibernate, if we try to access collection it triggers whole collection fetch.. so we must use
@BatchSize(size=10)

docker stack services stack_name

plain_content:
__proto__
As we all know there is no inheritance as we know generally in other languages
so javascript chains objects with __proto__
Now how an arr object gets Array behavior i.e how we can execute array methods on any Array object..??
So arr object's __proto__ points Array class in javascript so all its functions are now accessible by this new arr object, Array class's 
__proto__ points to Object class and as Object is root class for all its __proto__ points to null.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
so when we execute any function or property javascript first finds it on current object.. if its not there then walks the __proto__ hierarchy to find it
so as we know everything in javascript is an object , even functions are also object.

{"ops":[{"insert":"
Javascript Hoisting

Basically, when Javascript compiles all of your code, all variable declarations using var are hoisted/lifted to the top 
of their functional/local scope (if declared inside a function) or to the top of their global scope 
(if declared outside of a function) regardless of where the actual declaration has been made. 
This is what we mean by “hoisting”.

Functions declarations are also hoisted, but these go to the very top, 
so will sit above all of the variable declarations.


If we were to write the following in our global scope:
console.log(myName);
var myName = ‘Sunil’;

Pop quiz! What do you think the console.log will output?

1. Uncaught ReferenceError: myName is not defined
2. Sunil
3. undefined


It turns out that this third option is actually the correct answer.

However, a key thing to note is that the only thing that gets moved to the top is the variable declarations ,
 not the actual value given to the variable.

So Hoisting looks like this:

var myName;
console.log(myName); <-- prints undefined
myName = ‘Sunil’;

This is why the console.log is able to output ‘undefined’, because it recognises that the variable myName exists, 
but myName hasn’t been given a value until the third line.

--------

var, let, const, function and class declarations are hoisted.

----------

The difference between var, let and const declarations is their initialisation.

Instances of var and let can be initialised without a value (and if you try to call it, it will return undefined) 
while const will throw a Reference error if you try to declare one without assigning it a value at the same time.
So const myName = 'Sunil' would work, but const myName; myName = 'Sunil'; would not.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

So is there any difference between var, let and const in terms of hoisting?

Yes, if you create a var at the top level (global level), it would create a property on the global object — 
in the case of a browser, this is likely to be the window object. So creating var myName = 'Sunil'; 
can also be referenced by calling window.myName.

However, if you wrote let newName = 'Sunny'; this would not be accessible in the global window object 
— therefore, you would not be able to use window.newName as a reference to 'Sunny'

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
"}]}

plain_content:
OAuth
Key Points:
There is an Auth server and Resource server. Resource server can be only accessed once you get JWT oauth token,
Given though Header : Authorization=Bearer <..some token val >, this token contains upto what level you can access data
something like allowed roles.
Auth server exposes 3 urls :
/authorize used to get either authorization code or access token directly depending on flow used,
/token : used to get access token if not given previously,
/refresh : used to get new access token by giving refresh token as input.
OAuth is authorization protocol, OpenID is authentication protocol which returns IDToken a special type of token
containing user information.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Why OAuth:
Because you dont want to enter your credentials on some 3rd party server just to give access to your resource..
eg. you need to give your Instagram photos access to some 3rd party server
so you dont want to give Instagram username & password to that server, you just want Instagram to give your photos access to that server
This is where we need oauth. OAuth is authorisation protocol its not for Authentication, it solves delegated authorization problem.
Front Channel : Request from browser, mobile.. from user's own device
Back channel : Request from back end
Grant Types:
3 legged means , we need 3 steps to get resource
2 legged means we need 2 steps to resource
Grant Type: Authorization code :
First application owner register's app & it gets client ID and client secret
Step 1: Authorization Code Link
https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/authorize?
response_type=code
&client_id=CLIENT_ID
&redirect_uri=CALLBACK_URL
&scope=read
Here is an explanation of the link components:
		https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/authorize: the API authorization endpoint
  *  client_id=client_id: the application’s client ID (how the API identifies the application)
  *  redirect_uri=CALLBACK_URL: where the service redirects the user-agent after an authorization code is granted
  *  response_type=code: specifies that your application is requesting an authorization code grant
  *  scope=read: specifies the level of access that the application is requesting (this can be anything.. application specifies this, its like role)
Step 2: User Authorizes Application
When the user clicks the link, they must first log in to the service, to authenticate their identity (unless they are already logged in). Then they will be prompted by the service to authorize or deny the application access to their account. Here is an example authorize application prompt:
Step 3: Application Receives Authorization Code
If the user clicks “Authorize Application”, the service redirects the user-agent to the application redirect URI, which was specified during the client registration, along with an authorization code. The redirect would look something like this (assuming the application is “dropletbook.com”)
https://dropletbook.com/callback?
code=AUTHORIZATION_COD
Step 4: Application Requests Access Token ( as this is back end call we can safely pass client_secret.. as client_secret has ultimate access to get access tokens so we need to secure this.. we can't share this to anyone not even browser that's why its separate back end call)
The application requests an access token from the API, by passing the authorization code along with authentication details, including the client secret, to the API token endpoint. Here is an example POST request to DigitalOcean’s token endpoint:
https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/token?
client_id=CLIENT_ID
&client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET
&grant_type=authorization_code
&code=AUTHORIZATION_CODE
&redirect_uri=CALLBACK_URL
Step 5: Application Receives Access Token
If the authorization is valid, the API will send a response containing the access token (and optionally, a refresh token) to the application. The entire response will look something like this:
{
    "access_token": "ACCESS_TOKEN",
    "token_type": "bearer",
    "expires_in": 2592000,
    "refresh_token": "REFRESH_TOKEN",
    "scope": "read",
    "uid": 100101,
    "info": {
        "name": "Mark E. Mark",
        "email": "mark@thefunkybunch.com"
    }
}
Now the application is authorized! It may use the token to access the user’s account via the service API, limited to the scope of access, until the token expires or is revoked. If a refresh token was issued, it may be used to request new access tokens if the original token has expired.
====================================================================================================
Grant Type: Implicit ( only client ID passed with api , client secret is not passed.. )
The implicit grant type is used for mobile apps and web applications (i.e. applications that run in a web browser), where the client secret confidentiality is not guaranteed. The implicit grant type is also a redirection-based flow but the access token is given to the user-agent to forward to the application( front end, there is no back end server ), so it may be exposed to the user and other applications on the user’s device. Also, this flow does not authenticate the identity of the application, and relies on the redirect URI (that was registered with the service) to serve this purpose.
The implicit grant type does not support refresh tokens.
The implicit grant flow basically works as follows: the user is asked to authorize the application, then the authorization server passes the access token back to the user-agent which uses this to get resource directly from browser ( no back end call ).
Step 1: Implicit Authorization Link
With the implicit grant type, the user is presented with an authorization link, that requests a token from the API. This link looks just like the authorization code link, except it is requesting a token instead of a code (note the response type “token”):
https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/authorize?
response_type=token
&client_id=CLIENT_ID
&redirect_uri=CALLBACK_URL
&scope=read
Step 2: User Authorizes Application
When the user clicks the link, they must first log in to the service, to authenticate their identity (unless they are already logged in). Then they will be prompted by the service to authorize or deny the application access to their account. Here is an example authorize application prompt:
Step 3: User-agent Receives Access Token with Redirect URI
If the user clicks “Authorize Application”, the service redirects the user-agent to the application redirect URI, and includes a URI fragment containing the access token. It would look something like this:
https://dropletbook.com/callback#
token=ACCESS_TOKEN
Step 4: Access Token Passed to Application
The user-agent uses this token to access resource
========================================================================================================
Grant Type: Resource Owner Password Credentials ( generally used in android apps )
With the resource owner password credentials grant type, the user provides their service credentials (username and password) directly to the application, which uses the credentials to obtain an access token from the service. This grant type should only be enabled on the authorization server if other flows are not viable. Also, it should only be used if the application is trusted by the user (e.g. it is owned by the service, or the user’s desktop OS).
After the user gives their credentials to the application, the application will then request an access token from the authorization server. The POST request might look something like this:
https://oauth.example.com/token?grant_type=password
&username=USERNAME
&password=PASSWORD
&client_id=CLIENT_ID
If the user credentials check out, the authorization server returns an access token to the application. Now the application is authorized!
========================================================================================================
Grant Type: Client Credentials ( generally used for internal microservices to microservices call )
The client credentials grant type provides an application a way to access its own service account. Examples of when this might be useful include if an application wants access other data stored in its service account via the API.
The application requests an access token by sending its credentials, its client ID and client secret, to the authorization server. An example POST request might look like the following:
https://oauth.example.com/token?
grant_type=client_credentials
&client_id=CLIENT_ID
&client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET
If the application credentials check out, the authorization server returns an access token to the application. Now the application is authorized to use its own account!
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Difference bet'n client credentials flow vs Resource owner flow
both are backend flows
Resource owner flow :
Suppose you're a statistics company called AllStats that has its own user base 
where each user has their own username and password. AllStats has its own existing website. 
However, AllStats now wants to release a mobile app.
Since the mobile app will be a 1st party application (ie developed by AllStats), 
the Resource Owner Password Flow makes a lot of sense. You'll want the user to get a screen (username, password) 
that flows with the app instead of kicking them over to an auth server (and then back into the app). 
Users will trust the application when they enter their username/password because it's a 1st party app.
Client credentials flow is use for microservice to microservice calls
=======================================================================================================
Now how to use Access token
Once the application has an access token, it may use the token to access the user’s account via the API, limited to the scope of access, until the token expires or is revoked.
Here is an example of an API request, using curl. Note that it includes the access token:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN""https://api.digitalocean.com/v2/$OBJECT" 
Assuming the access token is valid, the API will process the request according to its API specifications. If the access token is expired or otherwise invalid, the API will return an “invalid_request” error.
Refresh Token Flow
After an access token expires, using it to make a request from the API will result in an “Invalid Token Error”. At this point, if a refresh token was included when the original access token was issued, it can be used to request a fresh access token from the authorization server.
Here is an example POST request, using a refresh token to obtain a new access token:
https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/token
?grant_type=refresh_token&
client_id=CLIENT_ID
&client_secret=CLIENT_SECRET
&refresh_token=REFRESH_TOKEN
========================================================================================================
Misuse of OAuth for login i.e Authentication purpose.. thats why OpenID is built :
Authentication Use case :
The only difference between normal OAuth and OpenID req. is openid asks ID Token, a special type of token that's it. Its similar in steps as Auth code grant but just it asks special ID Token
Using access token is optional , only used if we want more info about user, basic details are already there in ID Token
Sample Open ID request:
Now If we are not satisfied with the info in ID Token then we can use access token also came with ID Token and get more info.
ID Token is not encrypted its just Base64 formatted string, using signature we can verify integrity of it. ( See JSON Web Token notes..for how signature gets generated.. )
==========================================================================================================
Authentication code : this is short lived code usually valid for 1 min only used to retrieve access token (which is also short lived but lives more than Authentication token.. ) & usually can be used only once..
Access Token Types:
Reference Tokens : This needs to be validated through Auth servers, in return auth server sends back JWT
Self Contained Tokens ( usually JWT ) : These have everything a token should have and through signature we validate these
These can be sent by header, post body or as url param
signature is recomputed at server end to validate integrity, as server only have secret text only we can generate / test signature validity
Refresh Token : Used when client needs access for long period of time eg. days, weeks.. using this token client can get access token multiple times but whether to issue this token or not is up to Authorization server.
=======================================================================================================
Code Injection Attack / Auth code Interception Attack & why we need PKCE :
This is attack on Auth code flow, as Auth code goes through browser to backend, attacker captures it using malicious browser plugin installed in user's browser, so now it uses it to get access token.
As Auth code must be used only once.. backend doesn't gets Access token so user is not logged in.
So he tries again & now as user is already logged in, he directly gets Auth code and gets Auto logged in. So he think this as simple glitch.
So How PKCE prevents it ??
Now in PKCE the user which wants to get Access token has to prove he it the one who request Auth code in previous step.
code_verifier = this is uniq string
code_challenge = hashed form of code_verifier
code_challenge_method = this is string that tells which also is used to convert code_verifier to code_challenge ( eg. SHA 256 )
So before giving call to get Auth code, backend generates random string for code_verifier and hashes it with eg. SHA 256 and now this code_challenge sent along with normal Auth code request. Now as Hash is one way function attacker can capture it but can't get original code_verifier string & backend only gave browser hashed form of code_verifier so only backend know original code_verfier.
Now auth server gives Auth code and in its own memory remembers that AuthCode & code_challenge pair.
So at the time of getting Access token user must give original plain text code_verifier, so Auth server uses code_challenge_method to convert this code_verifier to code_challenge i.e hashes it and compare hashes if they match then Access token is given. ( Here as attacker can't get Plain text code_verifier from code_challenge he can't get Access token ,its mandatory to send PLAIN_TEXT code_verifier to get Access token)
So for every Auth code request we must use new uniq code_verifier.

Git
To create git repo in any folder :
git init
Now to have password less git login :
create ssh keys :
ssh-keygen -t rsa -C "ankushkale1@gmail.com"
this generates 2 files copy then to $HOME/.ssh so that ssh can auto pick them when required
copy contents of .pub file so that we can enable ssh login to Github, paste it as ssh key
ssh -T git@github.com => to test login
Now copy your git ssh url
git remote add origin git@github.com:ankushkale1/MyApps.git
git fetch
git pull
git push --all origin

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = KeycloakSecurityComponents.class)
class SecurityConfig extends KeycloakWebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {
    @Autowired
    public void configureGlobal(AuthenticationManagerBuilder auth) throws Exception {
        SimpleAuthorityMapper grantedAuthorityMapper = new SimpleAuthorityMapper();
        grantedAuthorityMapper.setConvertToUpperCase(true);
        grantedAuthorityMapper.setPrefix("ROLE_");
        
        KeycloakAuthenticationProvider keycloakAuthenticationProvider = keycloakAuthenticationProvider();
        keycloakAuthenticationProvider.setGrantedAuthoritiesMapper(grantedAuthorityMapper);
        auth.authenticationProvider(keycloakAuthenticationProvider);
    }
    @Bean
    public KeycloakSpringBootConfigResolver KeycloakConfigResolver() {
        return new KeycloakSpringBootConfigResolver();
    }
    @Bean
    @Override
    protected SessionAuthenticationStrategy sessionAuthenticationStrategy() {
        return new RegisterSessionAuthenticationStrategy(new SessionRegistryImpl());
    }
    @Override
    protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        super.configure(http);
        http
        .csrf().disable()
        .logout().logoutUrl("/logout").and()
        .authorizeRequests()
        .antMatchers("/user*").hasRole("USER")
        .antMatchers("/admin*").hasRole("ADMIN")
        .anyRequest().authenticated();
    }
}

Now Securing API by Keycloak
Let's say you have ServiceA and ServiceB. A user calls ServiceA which in hand calls ServiceB. ServiceB is never called by the user directly, only by other services. ServiceA will get a token using the user's credentials. And then will use this token to call ServiceB. ServiceB will never initiate a login. It will just use the token to verify permissions.
In this case, ServiceA will be confidential and ServiceB will be bearer-only clients.
Overall Flow:

Spring Boot Microservices Basics
What is a Microservice ?
Basic Problems while using Microservices Architecture :
1) How to break up Monolith to Microservices :
In this we try to identify what functionality Monolith does and how we can break up those in separate Microservices. (eg. using Domain Driven Design )
2) Configuration Management:
As there are many microservices are running how can we manage configuration, how we can propagate updated configuration, how to dynamically change configuration.
3) Dynamic Scale UP & Scale Down :
How to dynamically increase or decrease microservices, how to distribute load among them.
4) Visibility :
How microservices will know each other & how they will communicate with each other, how to know which microservice caused failure, how to trace problems in architecture.
5) Cascading Failure:
How to build fault tolerance in microservices so that one microservice doesn't bring down whole architecture.
Advantages of Microservices:
1) Flexibility in Choosing Tech :
For every service we can choose programming language, its architecture as per our requirement, so now we have freedom to choose what we want per microservice, we can quickly adopt new technology and process per microservice.
2) Dynamic Scaling :
We can dynamically increase or decrease microservice instances as per our requirement, so If we have load on one microservice we can increase its instances
3) Faster Release :
As each microservice only does some specific task we can quickly add, update features and release them
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Configuration Management
As We have multiple microservices, each microservices might have multiple environment active at a time.
So we need some centralized configuration management.
Spring Cloud Config Server:
Now we will use local git repository for this config server, so initialize local git repo in folder and we will add this folder path as config source.
Now in spring cloud projects spring.application.name is very important so never skip this in properties.
So here is the sample config for Config server with local git :
GET localhost:8888, GET localhost:8888/{some service name} has no bindings so gives 404
we must specify localhost:8888/{some service name}/{profile name}
so default profile is default ( which is {service name}.properties ),
all other profiles like dev should have {service name}-{profilename}.properties should present in git repo.
If profile prop file is not there then it will return default profile config.
Create a Project with Config client dependency :
Now notice we are not using application.properties we are using bootstrap.properties these gets loaded before application.properties
so we want config to be resolved before loading of anything so..
Now when we start config client, at very first spring will get config from config server so these are the very first messages.
Now 3 things are mandatory (not actually mandatory but should be there..) for Config client:
spring.application.name ,
spring.cloud.config.uri ,
spring.profiles.active
Now if we skip spring.application.name then default name is application so it will get empty properties, No error no exception
Now if we skip spring.cloud.config.uri
then 
it will try to connect to localhost:8888 ,
if config server is there then OK
else
application will still run but without those properties.
Now changes in git repo doesn't automatically propagated to microservices, we need to do restart for new changes.. which is headache so spring cloud bus is to notify these changes. ( that we will learn in next stages.. )
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Feign ( a kind of RestTemplate but much simpler than that.. & its Microservices aware.. )
Now Feign solves 2 problems:
1) Reduces complexity of calling a microservice ( just define interface with some annotation and that's it.. )
2) How to call multiple microservices with dynamic ( i.e on every restart port changes ) ports and which instance to call
Here is what we do using Rest Template Before Feign :

Now create a proxy:
Now ideally Feign should be used with Eureka & Ribbon but we are not configuring it now, so we need to manually provide url of service we are going to call through feign. We also need to specify url signature with standard spring controller way.
Now we can just use proxy and get response parsed in our POJO..
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ribbon ( Client side load balancing.. )
Now Feign is just a Microservices Aware RestTemplate, it needs someones help to know how many instances are there & which instance to call.
So Ribbon distributes load evenly across known microservices & gives instance to call to Feign. Ribbon distributes load default Round Robin.

Thats it.

=========================================================================================================
API Gateway Advantages :
ZUUL Setup :
Here is simple ZUUL logging filter :
Now in order to go through API Gateway, we only need to update url and Feign Client instance name.
Now as you have noticed that we didn't configure anything on ZUUL like URL forwarding, we didn't tell ZUUL that when you receive this URL redirect it to this microservice.. We just registered with Eureka, defined ourselves as Proxy and in other microservices they just changed
URL to call & Feign Instance name.
Now the @GetMapping we updated has convention so we should prefix old url with the spring.application.name of target service
Each request received by Zuul is forwarded to a different instance in a round robin fashion,
 everything is taken care by eureka and Zuul without any extra config.
========================================================================================================
Sleuth :
This attaches traceID with every uniq request.
Now in order to enable TraceID we need to include ( sleuth dependency & Sampler bean ) it in every microservice ( except Config & Eureka server )
Now if we log response in Some controller then we can see TraceID :
But as this is per microservice log, we have to check each microservice logs with specific TraceID, so we need centralized logs to better view,
so Zipkin is server for that.
===========================================================================================================
ZIPKIN ( Distributed Tracing server ) :
Now this is Centralized Logging, there are many ways to do this, eg. ELK stack, So we using ZIPKIN here..
So all microservice will be putting log in RabbitMQ and Zipkin will get it from there.. ZIPKIN stores these logs in DB, we will be using IN MEMORY DB.
So install RabbitMQ and start it. Now Zipkin server can be built as simple spring project or we can download prebuilt jar and start that.
So we tell Zipkin where is RabbitMQ by env variable.
Thats it Zipkin is started but now we need to tell other microservices to send logs to RabbitMQ.
So we need to ad these 2 dependencies to every microservice so that they can talk with RabbitMQ
Here sleuth-zipkin dependency is need to post messages in format that zipkin supports..
==========================================================================================================
Spring Cloud Bus :
Now when config changes, microservices didn't automatically fetch new config from config server, we have to manually call refresh
actuator endpoint on each microservice, so this is impractical so we need someone to push or notify updates to each microservice.
Now add this dependency in each service:
Disable security of Actuator in properties.
Now when config changes we just need to hit one url and every other application gets new config automatically
======================================================================================================
Hystrix (Circuit Breaker, Fault Tolerance, alternative Sentinel(Alibaba cloud) ) :
Why we need a Circuit breaker, why not just timeouts: Well timeout solves problem partly.. but still it will block thread and threads will eventually get piled up & we may end up exhausting system resources quickly once some microservice starts behaving abnormally.
So In Circuit breaker once it detects issue, it stops giving request to that server for a while, calls callback instead and after some cooling period
tries to call again.. if this time service is ok then continue using that.. else callback again for sometime.
Now if any error in default method then we can return value from fallback method so this will stop cascading failure.
So Hystrix Also works by Proxying actual class :
So if one method is calling another method in same class as its not going through proxy, hystrix doesn't work. (workaround is move that method to another class & autowire it and then call method.. )
Now Circuit breaker checks last 5 requests and if 3 have failed then it breaks circuit and for 10 sec calls fallback method and after that starts giving call to actual service.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Hystrix Isolation strategy.. ??
By default, the methods with @HystrixCommand will be executed on a different thread because the default
execution.isolation.strategy is ExecutionIsolationStrategy.THREAD.
So, the ThreadLocal variables we set before invoking @HystrixCommand methods won't be available
within @HystrixCommand methods.
One option to make the ThreadLocal variables available is using execution.isolation.strategy=SEMAPHORE.
@HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "getDefaultProductInventoryByCode",

   }
)
public Optional<ProductInventoryResponse> getProductInventoryByCode(String productCode)

plain_content:
GraphQL
Why GraphQL ?? ( in REST server decides what to give to client but in GraphQL user decides what he wants.. )
In typical rest response we either overfetch or underfetch data, so in GraphQL we can specify exactly what data we want using POST only request ( no GET,DELETE..), its querying like we do in sql. Here only one endpoint to get data not like multiple endpoints in rest to fetch different data.
As data is not verbose , only what we asked so performance is better than rest, also less network bandwidth and processing required.
Advantages:
 No overfetch or under fetching of Data : client specifies what he wants and gets only that.. nothing else..
Disadvantages:
1) In rest we can also request selective fields only
eg. GET /books/1492030716?fields=title,pageCount
2) In rest we can easily enforce rules on data types being posted from client.
3) In rest we can just check response status and we can know is it successful or not but in GraphQL we have to parse response to know. ( so response status will always be 200 )
4) Caching is difficult in GraphQL : In GraphQL, there’s only one endpoint (most of the time an HTTP POST endpoint) where all the queries are sent. Since each query can be different, it is harder to use this type of caching at GraphQL level

plain_content:
URL Shortening Service
Lets design url shortening service like TinyURL
Functional requirement :
1) input will be long url and output will be short url
2) we need to expire url after certain time
3) unique no. we generated must be collision free
4) system should be faster
There will be 2 main api's
1) URL shortening API that will take long url as input and return back short url
2) GET call on short url will redirect user to long actual url
Cache Size Estimation to cache frequently accessed urls :
Lets assume only anonymous user's scenario i.e user creation is not needed
According to nature of service NoSql database is best suited here.
To Generate Unique String :
1) We can use Hash like MD5 of original / input url and transform it using some
algorithm to 8-10 char unique no [0-9, a-z, A-Z] but this is runtime overhead and still we can't guarantee non collision property.
2) We can have separate Key Generation Service to pre-generate key for us in database and Whenever we want to shorten a URL, we will take one of the already-generated keys and use it. This approach will make things quite simple and fast. Not only are we not encoding the URL, but we won’t have to worry about duplications or collisions. KGS will make sure all the keys inserted into key-DB are unique.
Can concurrency cause problems? As soon as a key is used, it should be marked in the database to ensure that it is not used again. If there are multiple servers reading keys concurrently, we might get a scenario where two or more servers try to read the same key from the database. How can we solve this concurrency problem?
KSG will internally prefetch a set of keys in memory and it will return that set whenever some server exhausts keys.
Each url shortening server will prefetch keys from KSG and it will just assign user's url with that key and then will call DB service to update in batches or it will post that mapping to some central queuing service which DB service will consume and
store in database. As soon as KSG gives fresh key set to any server it will mark that set in DB as consumed.
So as we have large key space if KSG dies / restarts or any other url shortening server restarts those keys will be lost but thats ok. BY using queuing system like kafka we can increase no. of database service ( if there is master - master replication in db )
Now as our database will be quite big how we will divide our data or make our data faster ?
1) Range based partitioning so for eg. if unique no starts with A-D we store it in DB server 1, next range in Server 2 like that
but its possible that we overload some servers frequently.
2) Hash-Based Partitioning: In this scheme, we take a hash of the object we are storing. We then calculate which partition to use based upon the hash. In our case, we can take the hash of the ‘key’ or the short link to determine the partition in which we store the data object.
Our hashing function will randomly distribute URLs into different partitions (e.g., our hashing function can always map any ‘key’ to a number between [1…256]). This number would represent the partition in which we store our object.
This approach can still lead to overloaded partitions, which can be solved using Consistent Hashing.
Key Expiration :
1) Whenever a user tries to access an expired link, we can delete the link and return an error to the user.
2) A separate Cleanup service can run periodically to remove expired links from our storage and cache. This service should be very lightweight and can be scheduled to run only when the user traffic is expected to be low.
